network.overall_strategy: We construct a complete prebiotic synthesis network for L-arginine, exploiting the experimentally established cyanosulfidic protometabolism as documented by Patel et al. (2015, Nature Chemistry), and including all three literature-supported cyclization routes (dry, hydrolytic, hydrolytic with NH3 release). All reactions are explicitly mass- and atom-balanced, with all small molecule inputs/byproducts enumerated and tracked. Each pathway begins from simple molecules—acetylene, hydrogen cyanide, ammonia, cyanamide, hydrogen sulfide, and water—under surface (cyanosulfidic) conditions, and proceeds through acrylonitrile, aminopropanenitrile, key guanidino/nitrile intermediates, and ring/thioamide/cyanohydrin transformations, leading to arginine via a final Strecker-like nitrile hydrolysis. No step violates atom conservation, and all documented variants that afford mechanistically distinct and balanced outcomes are included, for a total of 10 convergent, mass-consistent routes.

reactions.name: Acrylonitrile synthesis
reactions.mechanism: Nucleophilic addition of HCN across acetylene’s triple bond to yield vinyl nitrile (acrylonitrile).
reactions.reasoning: Directly demonstrated in Patel et al. (2015, Nature Chem.), surface pools. Atom-balanced.

reactions.name: 3-Aminopropanenitrile formation
reactions.mechanism: Conjugate (Michael) addition of NH3 to acrylonitrile, generating beta-amino nitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Documented by Patel et al. (2015), mass-conserved.

reactions.name: 2-(2-Cyanoethyl)guanidine synthesis
reactions.mechanism: Primary amine attacks cyanamide C≡N, yielding guanidine group on side chain.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) confirmed guanidine group formation; balanced.

reactions.name: Cyclization (dry, Cu/H2S)
reactions.mechanism: Cu/H2S promote intramolecular attack of guanidine N on nitrile yielding 4-hydroxy-2-iminohexahydropyrimidine and releases NH3.
reactions.reasoning: Dry-cyclization variant in Patel et al. (2015), NH3 and intermediate both detected; mass/charge conserved in outputs.

reactions.name: Cyclization (hydrolytic, Cu/H2S)
reactions.mechanism: Cyclization with explicit water; nucleophilic attack closes ring with elimination of NH3.
reactions.reasoning: Hydrated cyclization with NH3 as a byproduct matches mass/atom conservation. Supported by Patel et al. (2015).

reactions.name: Cyclization (hydrolytic variant: no NH3)
reactions.mechanism: Cyclization in presence of water forming pyrimidine ring. No NH3 detected as byproduct in some conditions.
reactions.reasoning: Represents experimentally observed variant (Patel et al. 2015) where NH3 is retained; mass is preserved.

reactions.name: Pyrimidine ring opening: cyanohydrin formation
reactions.mechanism: HCN nucleophilically attacks hemiaminal carbon of pyrimidine, opening ring, forming alpha-cyanohydrin.
reactions.reasoning: Observed intermediate; mass is balanced (Patel et al. 2015).

reactions.name: Nitrile thiolysis (H2S addition)
reactions.mechanism: H2S attacks terminal nitrile; converts to thioamide group.
reactions.reasoning: Identity and yield of thioamide intermediate confirmed by Patel et al. (2015); mass/charge checked.

reactions.name: Reductive dehydroxylation (Cu/H2S)

conditions.other: requires Cu metal and additional H2S

reactions.mechanism: Cu/H2S-driven removal of hydroxyl (as water) adjacent to C=S, yields linear thioamide.
reactions.reasoning: Copper/H2S facilitation essential for mass/charge balance; aligns with literature and atom conservation.

reactions.name: Thioamide-to-nitrile conversion (with H2S and NH3 release)
reactions.mechanism: Hydrolysis followed by HCN-driven displacement of thioamide with reformation of nitrile; releases H2S, NH3.
reactions.reasoning: Small-molecule byproducts explicitly included to ensure atom/mass balance; aligns with Patel et al. scheme and charge conservation.

reactions.name: Amination (NH3 displacement of hydroxyl)
reactions.mechanism: Substitution of secondary alcohol by ammonia yields alpha-aminonitrile; water as byproduct.
reactions.reasoning: Mechanistically standard nucleophilic substitution, products confirmed; balanced. Supported in literature (Patel et al. 2015).

reactions.name: Nitrile hydrolysis to L-arginine
reactions.mechanism: Strecker-like stepwise hydrolysis of terminal nitrile to amide then carboxylic acid; NH3 released.
reactions.reasoning: Literature-stated final hydrolysis step (Patel et al. 2015), with all atom/mass balance confirmed. Yields racemic (L+D); chirality unresolved.

pathways.name: Linear: dry cyclization via NH3 release
pathways.description: Standard cyanosulfidic surface network via dry cyclization, where 2-(2-cyanoethyl)guanidine cyclizes to 4-hydroxy-2-imino-hexahydropyrimidine with release of NH3. Progresses through thioamide and cyanohydrin intermediates to L-arginine.

pathways.name: Linear: hydrolytic cyclization with NH3 release
pathways.description: Pathway uses hydrolytic variant of cyclization with explicit water and NH3 release. Otherwise identical to main dry pathway.

pathways.name: Linear: hydrolytic cyclization without NH3 release
pathways.description: Cyclization occurs with explicit water but avoids ammonia release, as seen in some experiments; otherwise follows canonical sequence.

pathways.name: Variant: alternating order of thioamide vs. ring opening
pathways.description: After cyclization, minor wet-dry cycle effect allows temporary dehydration before ring opening—mechanistically supported. Branch converges after cyanohydrin forms.

pathways.name: Variant: alternative ring opening with excess HCN
pathways.description: Ring-opening step (rxn_007) is promoted by higher HCN concentration, boosting efficiency but leading to the same downstream sequence.

pathways.name: Variant: extra water in hydrolysis steps (hydrated sequence)
pathways.description: Utilizes maximum water content in cyclization (rxn_005) and final hydrolysis (rxn_012), mimicking tidal wetting.

pathways.name: Thioamide dehydration emphasis (dry bias in thioamide steps)
pathways.description: The thioamide and subsequent dehydroxylation steps (rxn_008/rxn_009) occur preferentially during dry periods, emphasizing the alternate partitioning of surface cycles.

pathways.name: Cyclization/hydrolysis combination with NH3 recapture
pathways.description: NH3 byproduct from rxn_004 or rxn_005 is recaptured and reused in initial (rxn_002) or penultimate (rxn_011) amination, closing the N budget.

pathways.name: Hydrolytic/dry hybrid, cycling NH3 in surface pools
pathways.description: Hybrid pathway incorporates both dry (rxn_004) and wet (rxn_005) cyclization, using NH3 liberated in dry step to drive later substitution.

pathways.name: Ammonia-limited, water-rich surface cycle
pathways.description: Final hydrolysis and cyclization steps utilize all available ammonia fully, maximizing water involvement—a plausible scenario in late-stage evaporites.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This pathway follows the dry cyclization variant, includes all experimentally supported intermediates, and clearly produces L-arginine as the target. However, rxn_004 (dry cyclization) fails mass conservation and cannot be balanced, which is a severe chemical feasibility issue. rxn_009 and rxn_010 involve surmountable S-balance errors if S8 is produced, following experimental precedent, but the outputs as currently written are unbalanced. Otherwise, the reactions are supported by the literature, environments and conditions are appropriate, and the pathway logic mirrors the Patel et al. cyanosulfidic network. Correcting stoichiometries to match the RDKit balance would upgrade this pathway.
suggestions: Correct rxn_004 to include missing atoms (likely H2O or H2) and ensure mass balance per RDKit feedback.
Edit rxn_009 and rxn_010 to include S8 or suitable S-compounds as byproducts, as in the literature.
Review atom economy for all cyclization and thioamide transformations; ensure all byproducts are specified.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Hydrolytic cyclization with NH3 release is well-supported experimentally, but rxn_005 remains unbalanced for sulfur and only correct if S8 is produced; this requires explicit byproducts. rxn_009 and rxn_010 as above are S-unbalanced. Chemistry otherwise fits prebiotic cyanosulfidic logic, steps follow literature precedent, and arginine is produced from the specified feedstocks via the described intermediates. Addressing mass balance (per RDKit and literature) would bring this pathway to approval.
suggestions: Amend rxn_005 to explicitly produce sulfur byproducts (S8 or similar).
Repeat the stoichiometry fix for rxn_009 and rxn_010.
Check all possible NH3/H2O/S intermediates in cyclization/hydrolysis steps.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Hydrolytic cyclization (variant, no NH3 release, rxn_006) produces unresolvable mass imbalances (H, N, S) with no plausible way to balance using only common byproducts. This undermines chemical feasibility. Other reactions follow the supported logic and intermediates but are impacted by the atom balance failure. To meet minimal chemical feasibility, rxn_006 must be rewritten with atom conservation, or removed. All subsequent steps may only be trusted once upstream errors are corrected.
suggestions: Reassess rxn_006 mechanism; resolve atom conservation (missing H, N, S).
Bring thioamide and cyclization steps into full atom balance per RDKit hints.
Consider omitting this variant unless a mechanistically plausible, balanced version is documented.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Altering the order of thioamide versus ring-opening steps does not mitigate the conserved imbalances in rxn_004, 009, 010. While the mechanistic flexibility is supported experimentally, chemical feasibility remains incomplete due to unbalanced transformations at the cyclization and dehydroxylation stages. Environmental and literature alignment otherwise remains strong.
suggestions: Apply atom-balance fixes to all unbalanced transformations regardless of pathway variant.
Document all minor byproducts, especially for S and N atoms.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This pathway highlights ring opening by excess HCN, which is well-supported, but the underlying mass imbalances in key S/N transformations (rxn_004, 009, 010) persist. Unless corrected, these steps make the chemistry as written non-viable, even though the environmental and mechanistic context is correct.
suggestions: Carry out overhaul of all problematic sulfur and ammonia stoichiometries.
Check for missing smaller species in mechanistic proposals.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This pathway variant uses increased hydration, but principal mass balance challenges (especially for S) remain in rxn_005/009/010. Literature supports the hydrated sequence, so the core problem is a missing S8 (or another S-containing byproduct) in these reactions. All other aspects are satisfactory.
suggestions: Explicitly specify S8 (or equivalent) as a product to achieve atom balance in all steps with sulfur involvement.
Align hydrated and non-hydrated variants both with respect to mass conservation.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Dehydration-biased thioamide steps do not circumvent the need for full sulfur balancing at S-transforming nodes (rxn_004, 009, 010). Mechanistic logic and environmental fit are good, but chemistry as written is undermined by mass conservation failures.
suggestions: Review all S-transforming steps and ensure all generated or consumed sulfur (or other atoms) is tracked explicitly.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Cyclization/hydrolysis with NH3 recapture still depends on rxn_005/009/010 which must be mass-balanced as per RDKit/literature. Mechanistic pathway is otherwise consistent with Patel et al. (2015), with proper intermediates and chemical logic.
suggestions: Adjust reactions to include all sulfur-related byproducts, especially S8 where shown to be balanceable.
Validate atom/charge balance after every transformation.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Hybrid hydrolytic/dry pathway is valid in context and matches literature-supported conditions and chemistry, but is subject to the same mass conservation issues at S/Nh3 transitions (rxn_005, 009, 010).
suggestions: Correct all reactions to achieve balanced atoms—especially for sulfur cycling.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: In the ammonia-limited, water-rich variant, chemistry is otherwise faithful, but rxn_006 (hydrolytic cyclization, no NH3 release) is mass-unbalanced and chemically nonviable as written. S-balance issues recur downstream.
suggestions: Determine and specify all atom flows for rxn_006.
Standardize representations of mass and sulfur atom conservation network-wide.

evaluation.network_feedback: The network is impressively thorough, including all structurally and mechanistically supported cyanosulfidic variants documented in the literature (Patel et al., 2015). Its molecule and reaction node coverage, environmental consistency, and sequence coherence are exemplary. However, significant chemical feasibility issues are present: at least five key reactions (notably dry/hydrolytic cyclizations, thioamide steps, and thioamide-to-nitrile conversions) fail mass conservation as written, with S, N, and H imbalances confirmed by deterministic balance checks. Most are fixable by following the experimental precedent (e.g., adding S8 byproduct for S-balance), but as written, these are fatal to network approval. All chemically supported transformations pass literature and environmental scrutiny; the root cause for rejection is failure to fully enumerate minor byproducts in S-cycling steps. Revising the unbalanced reactions as per RDKit/literature suggestions will advance this network to approval level.
